note:
Ша̏тровачкӣ is a slang in which the syllables of a word are swapped:
• бра̏те - тебра
• пази - зипа
• ка̀фа - фука
• пи̑во - вопи
• гла́ва - вугла
• здра̏во - воздра

The word ша̏тро itself means «supposedly»: the language was built so that people seem to speak normally, but only insiders understand.

Nicknames are formed the same way: Милош - Лошми, Никола - Џони, Данило - Чода, Владимир - Довла.
title: Шатровачки: the syllable-swap slang

note:
At the end of a greeting or a phrase, friends often add an affectionate, joking form of address: бра̏те, ма̑јсторе, легендо, ца̏ре.

They do not necessarily mean a relative or a profession, they just stress closeness. You can translate them as «dude», «bro», «buddy».

These are vocative forms:
• бра̏т - бра̏те
• ма̑јстор - ма̑јсторе
• лѐге̄нда - легендо
• ца̏р - ца̏ре
title: How friends address each other

note:
Computer vocabulary has English loanwords (фа̑јл, пасворд, скриншот) and native words side by side. The Serbian version often exists and is in use:
• датоте́ка - file
• ло̀зӣнка - password
• на́лог - account
• претражѝвач - browser
• снимак екрана - screenshot
• обавѐште̄ње - notification
• нежељена пошта - spam
• резервна копија - backup
• преу̀зе̄ти - to download

The English loanwords are handy in conversation, but the Serbian words are better to know for documents and interfaces.
title: English loanwords in IT and their Serbian replacements

related.en: wedding guest (of the groom's or bride's side)

note:
Among the traditional wedding customs:
• гађање јабуке - the groom shoots at an apple on the roof
• the «buying out of the bride» by the wedding guests
• ломљење погаче - whoever breaks off the bigger piece will be the head of the family
• decorating the wedding cars
• carrying the bride over the threshold

The toasts (здравице) are made by the ку̑м. Some of the customs are more of a joke today, but the words сва̑т, ку̑м, по̀гача, младѐнци come up all the time.
title: Serbian wedding customs

note:
Even native speakers find words with a heap of consonants hard. The real «jaw-breakers»:
• усре̏дсредити, посластѝчарница, ра̀јсфершлус
• ратнохушкачки, пр̀тља̄г, цвр́чак, стр̏шље̄н

The record holder is ра̀јсфершлус. For practice, learn the words as a whole, not syllable by syllable.
title: Serbian tongue-twister words

note:
Collective nouns denote a mass of things as one whole. They are singular:
• neuter: др̀ве̄ће, ли̑шће, ка̀ме̄ње, гра̑ње
• feminine - names of young animals ending in -ад: пѝлад, ја̏гња̄д, те̏ла̄д, пра̏сад

Such words do not combine with numerals.
title: Collective nouns

note:
ID documents:
• лична карта - national ID card
• па̑сош - passport

Papers:
• по̏тврда - certificate confirming a fact
• увере́ње - official certificate, for example of citizenship
• и̏звод - extract (from a register)
• и̏зјава - statement, declaration
• у̀платница - payment slip
• призна̀ница - receipt

A letter can be о̀бично (regular) or препоручено (registered).
title: Words for documents and papers

note:
The short words па, зна̑чи, ми̏слӣм, е̏во, ма̏, ба̏ш, она̀ко̄ mean little by themselves, but make a remark lively:
• па - hesitation: «па... мо̀жда»
• зна̑чи - summing up: «значи, закаснио је»
• ми̏слӣм - clarifying: «ми̏слӣм, нѝје ло̏ше»
• е̏во - here
• ма̏ - come on
• ба̏ш - really, very
• она̀ко̄ - so-so

Without them, speech sounds dry.
title: Filler words that «color» speech

note:
Ћа̏ле (dad) and ке̏ва (mom) are popular words of youth slang.

Where they come from:
• ке̏ва - from кевац («father») in шатровачки, the Belgrade back slang, with the meaning shifted from father to mother, or from Hebrew, via the speech of the Sephardim in Belgrade's До̏рчол
• ћа̏ле - according to linguists, an adaptation of the word ћаћа, which is what a father is called in Dalmatia and Lika
title: Ћале and кева: where «dad» and «mom» come from

note:
Variable parts of speech:
• и̏меница - noun
• при́дев - adjective
• бро̑ј - numeral
• за̑меница - pronoun
• гла̏гол - verb

Invariable:
• пре́длог - preposition
• при́лог - adverb
• ре̏чца - particle
• ве̑знӣк - conjunction
• у̏звӣк - interjection

These terms appear in textbooks and in class, so it is handy to know them in advance.
title: Parts of speech in Serbian

note:
Punctuation marks:
• та̏чка, за̀рез (or за̀пета), две тачке, та̏чка-за̀рез
• на̀водници, заграде
• у̀питнӣк, у̀звичник
• цр̏та - dash, цр̏тица - hyphen

In speech, the @ sign is called ма̀јмунче, «little monkey».
title: Punctuation marks in Serbian

note:
Useful words:
• ши̏ша̄ње - haircut, ши̏шке - bangs, паж - bob
• фени̏ра̄ње - blow-dry, шати́ра̄ње - highlights
• фарбање праменова - coloring strands
• прање косе - hair washing

A clipper cut down to zero is «шишање машиницом на нулу», and scissors only is «само маказама». Clipper guard numbers, as in English («a number three»), are «на ке̑ц, двојку, тројку».
title: At the hairdresser's

note:
Almost five centuries of Ottoman rule left many words:
• са̑т, па̏ре, ка̀фа, ча̀рапа, ја̀стук, џе̏п
• ко̀мшија, ка̀пија, ба́шта, то́рба, шѐћер, ра̀кија, за̀на̄т

Turkish particles also live in speech:
• ха̀јде / а̀јде - come on
• ва̀јда - use, benefit: «нема вајде»
• јо̏к - no, colloquial

Knowing these words makes Turkish words easier to recognize.
title: Turkisms in Serbian

note:
On November 11, Serbia marks Да̑н прѝмирја, the day of the armistice that ended the First World War. There are ceremonies, wreaths (ве́нац) are laid, and a minute of silence (мѝнӯт ћу̀тања) is observed.

The country's losses were enormous, about a quarter of the population.

The symbol of the day is the ramonda flower, a species listed in the Red Book of endangered plants.
title: Armistice Day in Serbia

note:
Serbian names relatives more precisely than English does:
• стри̑ц - paternal uncle, his wife is стри̑на
• у̏ја̄к - maternal uncle, his wife is у̏јна
• брата̀нац - nephew, brother's son
• се̏стрић - nephew, sister's son

Parents of spouses:
• свѐкар and све̏крва - the husband's
• та̏ст and та̏шта - the wife's

При̏ја (also при̏јатељ and прика) are the parents of a married couple, as they call each other.

Сла̏ва is the main family holiday, the day of the family's patron saint.
title: Relatives in Serbian

note:
A typical selection at a Serbian bakery:
• bread: бе̑лӣ хле̏б, цр̑нӣ хле̏б, по̀гача, про̀ја
• pastries: ки́фла, ђѐврек, бу̏хтла
• filled: гѝбаница, пи̏та, бу̀рек
• sweet: кро́фна, штру́дла, слатка пита with apples or sour cherries

Бу̀рек can be пра́зан (plain, without filling), with cheese or with meat. In Bosnia бу̀рек is only the meat kind, and the rest is called пи̏та.
title: At a Serbian bakery

note:
In the Catholic communities of Vojvodina, December 6 is Ми̏кулаш, the feast of Saint Nicholas.

According to the legend, he arrives on a white horse the evening before and puts gifts (по̀клон) into the children's shoes on the window sill. Children polish their boots (чи̏зма) and put them on the window sill, and in return they are expected to behave well and get good grades.
title: Микулаш in Vojvodina

related.sr: би̏о је бо̏лестан, па нѝје до̏шао
related.en: he was sick, so he didn't come

note:
Cause:
• је̏р, за̀то̄ што̏ - because

Effect:
• за̀то̄, сто̏га̄, због тога, о̀туда - therefore
• па - in speech: «био је болестан, па није дошао»

More formal: с обзиром на то, на основу тога, у складу с тим, у̏след чѐга.

You can add emphasis with у̏право за̀то̄, ба̏ш за̀то̄, за̀то̄ и - that is exactly why.
title: How to express cause and effect

note:
Бадњи дан falls on January 6, the eve of Orthodox Christmas.

In the morning, an oak branch, the ба̏дња̄к, is cut in the forest, and in towns it is bought near a church.

It is a fasting day: fish, beans, sauerkraut, walnuts.

In the evening, a bonfire is lit near the church and the ба̏дња̄к is put on it. Along with the бадњак, the по̀ложајник comes into the house.
title: Бадњи дан: Christmas Eve in Serbia

related.en: «Dream of the Virgin Mary» (a protective prayer)

related.sr: пу̏, пу̏ да те не у̏рекнем
related.en: ptooey, ptooey, so I don't jinx you

note:
To protect a baby from the у́рок:
• tie a red thread (црвени конац) on the wrist
• put a booklet «Сан Мајке Божије» in the crib
• put an undershirt on the baby inside out

Seeing a baby, Serbs affectionately say «јој, што̏ си ру́жан!» and add «пу, пу да те не урекнем».

It is customary to give money to the parents on the first visit, and it is better to accept a treat offered by a stranger.
title: Babies and the evil eye in Serbia

related.en: As many sparks, so much health!

note:
По̀ложајник is a guest who, according to belief, brings luck to the house. He is a man or, better still, a boy. He symbolizes the Magi from the East.

What he does:
1. Enters with the greeting «Христос се роди!»
2. Steps in with the right foot.
3. Stirs the fire with an oak twig to raise sparks and says: «Колико варница, толико здравља!» (ва̏рница - spark).
4. Finishes with the words «А̀мӣн, Бо̏же да̑ј!»

He does not eat anything before he comes to the house.
title: Положајник: the first guest at Christmas

note:
On the night before Christmas, in Vojvodina and in some parts of Belgrade, children go from house to house (коринђање), recite joking rhymes (коринђе) and shout «Је л' слободно коринђати?» («May we go caroling?»).

The hosts give out tangerines, apples, walnuts, candy and small change, and rakija to the adults.

Every year there are fewer carolers (коринђаши), and the housewives afterward discuss how many came.
title: Коринђање: caroling in Vojvodina

related.en: a shot dropped into a beer

note:
Serbian «cocktails»:
• шпри̏цер - white wine with soda water
• гѐмишт - white wine with mineral water
• ба̀мбус - red wine with cola
• по̀дмо̄рница («submarine») - a shot of rakija dropped into a mug of beer
• бушена вотка - vodka with juice, «punctured», that is, diluted

But usually both wine drinks are simply called шприцер.
title: Serbian «cocktails»

related.sr: Да бу̏де̄м здра̏в и ру̀мен ка̏о о̀ва̄ ја̏бука
related.en: May I be healthy and rosy-cheeked like this apple

related.sr: Да бу̏де̄м ја̑к ка̏о о̀ва̄ј ди̏на̄р од че̏лика
related.en: May I be strong like this steel dinar

note:
On Christmas morning the household washes with the red apple (ја̏бука) from Christmas Eve:
1. They rub it on the cheeks, forehead and chin and say: «Да бу̏де̄м здра̏в и ру̀мен ка̏о о̀ва̄ ја̏бука».
2. Then they do the same with a dinar coin, saying: «Да будем јак као овај динар од челика».
3. The coin is passed from hand to hand so that money keeps coming.

It is also customary to symbolically start a task that has not been going well.
title: Christmas morning: washing with an apple

note:
On the three Sundays before Christmas, family days are celebrated:
• Детинци - Children's Day, the third Sunday before Christmas
• Материце - Mothers' Day, the second Sunday
• О̀ци - Fathers' Day, the last Sunday

The person being honored is symbolically «tied up» and buys their way out with a smile, a song, a gift or a good deed.
title: Детинци, Материце, Оци

note:
In Serbia people speak Ekavian, while in Bosnia, Montenegro and Croatia they speak Ijekavian.

The difference goes back to the ancient sound «yat»:
• мле́ко - млијеко
• ле̑по - лијепо
• де́те - дијете
• ре̑ч - ријеч
• ле̏то - љето
• нѐдеља - недјеља

The words are the same, only the pronunciation and spelling differ.

The app's cards always use Ekavian.
title: Ekavian and Ijekavian

note:
On January 19, Serbs celebrate Богоја́вље̄ње - Epiphany.

What happens:
• in churches water is blessed (освештање воде) and taken home, where it is kept all year
• on the night of the feast, according to belief, the heavens open and you can make a wish
• unmarried girls put a small mirror under the pillow to see their future husband

The main custom is пли̏ва̄ње за ча̏снӣ кр̏ст: the Holy Cross (ча̏снӣ кр̏ст) is thrown into the river, and whoever fetches it first has luck for the whole year.
title: Богојављење and the swim for the Holy Cross

note:
In modern Serbian, feminine names of professions are formed like this:
• suffix -ка: дѝректорка, нови̏нарка, касирка, профѐсорка
• suffix -ица: учитѐљица, чиста̀чица, продава̀чица, коноба̀рица, пева̀чица
• suffix -киња: сту̀денткиња, јуна̀киња, пе̏сникиња, кнѐгиња, монахиња

The suffix -ка is the most common. One word can have several variants: профѐсорка, професорица, професоркиња.
title: Feminine forms of professions

note:
Austria-Hungary left many German loanwords in Serbian:
• фа̑рба, фла̏ша, ја̀кна, ко̀фер, ко́рпа
• штра̏јк, ша̀лтер, шми̑нка, шпо̏рет
• тѐпих, ци̏мер, ма̏нтил
• фа̏лити, капи́рати - colloquial

Once you recognize the German root, the meaning is easy to guess.
title: German words in Serbian

note:
Serbian names are shortened in their own way:
• Александар - Аца, Са̏ша
• Душан - Дуле
• Никола - Нидџа
• Петар - Пера
• Милан - Ми́ле, Мики
• Слободан - Боба
• Стефан - Стефи
• Јован - Јоца
• Драган - Дра̑гӣ

There are also «шатровачки» variants: the syllables are swapped, Владимир - Довла.

The variants depend on the region.
title: Diminutive forms of male names

related.en: dough fried and soaked in syrup

note:
How coffee is brewed and served:
• brewed in a copper џе̏зва
• served on a tray in a small cup (фѝлџа̄н) with a copper holder (за̏рф) and a sugar bowl

Served with the coffee:
• ра́тлук - Turkish delight, in Serbia without nuts
• ва̀нилице - cookies with jam
• тулумбе - dough in syrup

For Serbs, coffee is a ritual: conversation, gossip and stories.
title: Coffee, Serbian style

related.en: Swiss: a green tram from Basel
«Turk»: a nickname for the new trams that did not catch on
the center of Belgrade along the route of tram No. 2

note:
In Belgrade, trams are called not only by their number:
• old red ones - Че̏х or на̏ш
• modern red-and-blue ones - Шпа́нац
• green ones that came from Basel in 2001 - Швајцарац
• new blue ones brought from Turkey - simply нови. The name Ту̀рчин has not caught on yet

Круг двојке is the center of Belgrade along the route of tram No. 2.
title: Belgrade trams by their nicknames

note:
Many international words have a gender in Serbian that you have to learn. Most follow the ending: «-а» is feminine, a consonant is masculine, and сту̑дио and интѐрвјӯ are masculine too.

Feminine:
• сала́та, адрѐса, контро́ла, ка̀фа, кли́ма, гардеро́ба
• аро́ма, варија̀нта, ета̀па, анали́за, синте́за
• дијагно́за, ша̏нса, нија̀нса

Masculine:
• сту̑дио, про̀грам, интѐрвјӯ, дѐта̄љ, про̀бле̄м

Check the gender before you make an adjective agree: вѐликӣ про̀бле̄м, јака кафа.
title: Gender of loanwords

related.en: a name in its own right (literally «hope»)
a name in its own right (literally «dawn»)
a name in its own right (literally «rose»)

note:
Female names are shortened like this:
• Јелена - Је́ла, Јеца
• Милица - Мица
• Ивана - И́ва
• Катарина - Каћа, Ка́та
• Мирјана - Ми́ра
• Љиљана - Љиља
• Снежана - Снежа
• Ана - Анчи

Sometimes the short form is already a name in its own right: На́да, Зо̀ра, Ру́жа.

The variants depend on the region.
title: Diminutive forms of female names

note:
The particle бре̏ colors speech with emotion: from friendly closeness to irritation. Its origin is unclear.

Theories:
• a Turkish word meaning «fool»
• the Greek «βρε» as a form of address
• the Spanish hombre
• simply an emotional exclamation
• a contraction of бра̏те: брате - бр'те - бре

A related form of address is бато, from бра̏т.
title: Where «бре» comes from

note:
Names of nationalities are written with a capital letter: Ср̏бин, Ру̏с, Не́мац.

Feminine forms are most often made:
• with -ка: Италѝја̄нка, Ја̀па̄нка
• with -киња: Ру̏скиња, Ср̏пкиња, Францускиња
• with -ица: Нѐмица, Мађа̀рица

The plural often changes the consonant: Че̏х - Чеси, Гр̏к - Гр̏ци, Ту̀рчин - Ту̑рци.

An interesting fact: the nickname жабари («frogs») refers in Serbian to Italians, not to the French.
title: Nationalities in Serbian

note:
Serbs love genealogy (ро̀дослов) and can spend a long time working out who is related to whom, and in which generation.

Words:
• ро̏дбина - all the relatives
• по̀родично ста́бло - family tree
• ко̀лено - degree of kinship

Ancestors have separate names up to the 16th generation: чукундѐда and чукунба̀ба - great-great-grandfather and great-great-grandmother.
title: Serbs and genealogy

related.en: «Today is a wonderful day for us» (a birthday song)

note:
At a Serbian birthday party:
• the birthday person (сла̏вљеник) is congratulated: «Сре̏ћан ро̏ђенда̄н!»
• balloons (балони) are blown up and decorations are hung
• people give a по̀клон and a чѐститка
• the candles (свећице) on the cake are blown out with a wish

A must is the song «Да̀нас нам је ди̑ван да̑н»: it has its own melody and words, different from «Happy Birthday».
title: Birthdays in Serbian

related.en: Neoplanta, «new planting» (the name chosen by Maria Theresa)
Petrovaradin (the fortress across from Novi Sad)

note:
Novi Sad was founded in 1694 on the left bank of the Danube, because the Orthodox were not allowed to settle in Petrovaradin.

In 1748 the city became a free royal city, and Maria Theresa chose the name Неопланта.

Other names:
• Петроварадински шанац
• Рацка варош
• Hungarian Újvidék, German Neusatz

Novi Sad is called «Српска Атина».
title: Names of Novi Sad

related.en: to get up, to stand up
to pause, to stop for a moment

note:
The verb ста̑ти has many derivatives:
• у̀стати - to get up
• прѐстати - to stop, to cease
• на̀стати - to arise
• за̀стати - to pause, to stop for a moment
• о̀стати - to stay, to remain
• о̀пстати - to survive, to hold out
• до̀стати - to be enough
• по̀стати - to become
• прѝстати - to agree
• ра̀стати се - to part
• изо̀стати - to fail to appear

Prefixes change the meaning a lot, so it is best to learn them from examples.
title: Prefixes with «стати»

note:
Cats in Serbia are called with «мац-мац-мац», from the affectionate ма́ца.

To make a dog (па̏с) or a puppy (штѐне) come, you say «Дођи!»
title: Calling cats and dogs

note:
Singular only - mass and abstract words:
• пе́сак, мле́ко, шѐћер, бра̏шно, зла̑то, љу́бав, на̏мешта̄ј

Collective:
• дѐца, бра̏ћа, ли̑шће, госпо̀да

Plural only:
• ма̀казе, на̏оча̄ре, вра́та, ле́ђа, у́ста, плу́ћа, пр̏са
• ко̏ла, пантало́не, ја̏сле

Some geographic names are plural: Хаваји, Малдиви, Алпи.
title: Words used only in the singular or only in the plural

note:
The name of a rakija usually tells what it is made from:
• шљи̏вовица - plum
• кајсијевача, крушковача, ја̏буковача, дуњевача, лозова̀ча - apricot, pear, apple, quince, grape

With additions:
• траварица - herbs
• ораховача - walnuts
• медо̀вача - honey

The suffix -овача / -евача is added to the name of the fruit.

Rakija is drunk as a sign of hospitality, with the meal and on holidays, at room temperature (about 18-20 degrees Celsius). The word came from Arabic through Turkish.

Vessels: ка̀зан - still, чо̏кањ - small flask, ча̏шица - shot glass.
title: Rakija: kinds and customs

related.en: wedding party, the guests from the groom's side
wedding guest from the groom's side

title: A Serbian wedding: customs

note:
From French came:
• жу̑рка - party, from jour
• рѐшо̄, анкѐта, ле̏же̄ран, ша̏рм, рѝва̄л
• аве́нија, жалу̀зине, шампа́њац, па̏рдон

Some meanings are not what you might expect:
• гардеро́ба - clothes
• маши́на - machinery or an appliance
• паж - a «bob» haircut
• ру̑ж - lipstick
• шмизла - a fashionista
title: French words in Serbian

note:
Many cities sound different in Serbian:
• Мѝнхен, Па̀рӣз, Марсеј, Мила̑но, На́пуљ
• Бе̑ч, Бу̀димпешта, Брѝсел, Бу̏курешт, Пра̏г
• Дублин, Хавана, Шангај

Names of cities in the region:
• Ско̏пље, Битољ, Ати́на, Со̀лӯн
• Сегедин, Дебрецин, Печуј
title: City names in Serbian

related.en: the bohemian quarter of Belgrade with its кафане
«Three Hats», one of the oldest кафане of Скадарлија

note:
Кафа̀на is a Serbian tavern. In the past, writers, artists and actors gathered in it.

The center of bohemian life was in the кафана «Дарданели», later in the Скадарлија quarter, where «Три шешира» is one of the oldest. Among the bohemians were Ђура Јакшић, Радоје Домановић, Бора Станковић.

The word богема is from French bohème, and a member of the bohemia is a бо̀е̄м.
title: The кафана and Belgrade bohemia

note:
Words from Czech came into Serbian:
• ча̏сопӣс, у̏лога, чѝта̄нка, становни́штво, ге̏сло
• до́јам, до̀следан, пѝшто̄љ, ко̀пачка, скле̏к
• по̀во̄рка, о̀бред, пре̏дно̄ст, све̏ска, и̏скрен

The best-known international word of Czech origin is «ро̏бот».
title: Bohemisms: words from Czech

related.en: to fall for something; to show off

related.sr: Не мо̀гу, смо̀рио сам се да̀нас.
related.en: Can't, I'm kind of bored today.

note:
Heard in conversation:
• смо̏р - boredom, бле̏ја - hanging out, га̑с - fun, vibe
• бра̏те / брт - bro, ли̑к - guy
• ло̀жити се - to fall for something or to show off
• ци̏мати се - to stress out
• кри̏нџ (cringe), рандом (something random), ре̏а̄лно - actually, то̏п - great

Example: «Брате, ајде на блеју?» - «Не могу, сморио сам се данас» (Bro, wanna hang out? - Can't, I'm kind of bored today).
title: Everyday Serbian slang

note:
Traditional desserts of Serbia:
• ва̀нилице - cookies named one of the best in the world
• штрудле - especially in Banat
• салчићи - puff-pastry rolls with jam
• орасница - with walnuts
• Васина торта - from Paraćin
• облатне and бајадѐра, which is served on the слава
• кнедле with fruit - popular in the north of the country
title: Serbian sweets

note:
Кафа̀на is a traditional place of Serbian life: checkered tablecloths, wooden tables, ра̀кија, grilled meat (ћева̀пи), tamburitza players, requested songs and talk until late at night.

Famous examples are «Знак питања» in Belgrade and Скадарлија.

The word мѐра̄к belongs to its spirit - savoring the moment.
title: The кафана is more than a restaurant

related.en: a park and forest in Belgrade
a lake island park in Belgrade

note:
On May 1, Serbs go out into nature before dawn, often spending the night there the day before.

The word у̀ранак comes from the verb ра̏нити - to get up early. Ethnologists link the custom with the feast of Ђу̏рђевда̄н.

The classic set: ро̀штӣљ, ћева̀пи, sausages and dishes cooked in a cauldron. In Belgrade, Кошутњак, Ада Циганлија and Авала are popular.

Related words: ѝзлет, лѝвада.
title: The May Day «уранак»

note:
In Serbian the sound «р» can be the nucleus of a syllable, so there are words with no vowels at all:
• пр̏ст, кр̑в, тр̑н, тр̏г, гр̏м, смр̏т

Syllabic «р» also occurs in the middle of words:
• чвр̑ст, мр̏шав, пр̏сте̄н, стрпље́ње

It helps to pronounce them slowly, then faster - that way the tongue gets used to them.

Кр̏ш is a rock, and also a mess.
title: A syllable without a vowel: syllabic р

related.sr: Па, не зна̑м шта̏ да ра̏дим.
related.en: Well, I don't know what to do.

related.sr: О̀ва̄ј, зна̑ш, то̑ је би́ла до̀бра иде́ја.
related.en: Um, you know, that was a good idea.

note:
In spoken language Serbs often fill pauses with words:
• па, о̀ва̄ј, ми̏слӣм, зна̑чи, ка̏о, ви̏дӣш
• она̀ко̄, у суштини, за̏право, е̏то, ва̀ла̄

They soften a statement or give time to think. For example:
• «Па, не знам шта да радим» (Well, I don't know what to do)
• «Овај, знаш, то је била добра идеја» (Um, you know, that was a good idea)
title: Filler words in colloquial speech

note:
When posing for a photo, Serbs say «Чииз!» (from the English cheese) or «Пти̏чица!» (little bird).

The second word goes back to the time when a photographer got children's attention by promising that a little bird was about to fly out. It is still used.

To ask for a photo: «Можеш ли да ме сликаш?»

Related words: сли̏кати, фотогра̀фија, ка̏дар.
title: Птичица! - how people ask for a smile

note:
Serbian has its own «unit» for each food, much like English «a clove of garlic»:
• herbs and vegetables: лист босиљка, гранчица рузмарина, веза першуна, кли̑п кукуру́за, чен белог лука
• fruit and nuts: кришка јабуке, га̑јба мандари́на, шака бадема
• sacks: џа̑к кромпи́ра
• other: кугла сладоледа, парче пице, коцка шећера, прстохват соли

This helps in a store and in a recipe: it is immediately clear what portion is meant.
title: Names for portions of food

related.en: a river and canyon in southwestern Serbia

note:
Увац is a canyon (ка̀њо̄н) of the river in southwestern Serbia, a protected nature reserve where wild nature has been preserved.

What is here:
• griffon vultures soar all year round
• deep meanders (вијуге) between the mountains Зла̀та̄р and Јавор
• karst caves (пећине) and hiking trails
• viewpoints (видиковци)

The best time to go is the warm season.
title: Uvac Canyon

note:
In a number of words, «бран» (from бра́нити - to defend) means an object that protects against something:
• ки̏шобра̄н - from rain
• су̏нцобра̄н - from the sun
• па̏добра̄н - from falling
• ве̏тробра̄н - from wind
• гро̏мобра̄н - from thunder
• бла̏тобра̄н - from mud

The same verb is used when students «defend» a thesis: бранити дипломски рад. The defense itself is о̏дбрана.
title: The root «бран» - protection

related.en: «valley of hunger», joking nickname of Kragujevac

note:
Serbs like to give cities ironic nicknames:
• Земун - Мунзе
• Панчево - Панчестер
• Рума - Румстердам
• Врбас - Лас Врбас
• Чока - Чокаго
• Ниш - Нотин (a play on the word ни̏шта, «nothing»)

Some nicknames hint at the character of the city: Бор - Мордор, Крагујевац - Долина глади.

A fun trio of Belgrade suburbs (предграђа) - Овча, Борча, Крњача - together sounds like «ча-ча-ча».
title: Joking nicknames of Serbian cities

note:
Many everyday Serbian words are of foreign origin:
• пара̀дајз - from the German «paradise apple»
• шме̏к - from German schmecken
• ѝна̄т, џа̏бе̄, ба̀ксуз, мѐра̄к - via Turkish from Arabic and Persian

Such words carry a shade of emotion that neutral words lack.
title: Where words came from
